student_profile.student_background: Upper-primary school learners, ages 8-11 (Grades 4-6), in rural Kenyan community schools. Reading in English as a second language; no devices or internet access during learning — all materials are printed and fully self-contained.
student_profile.aggregate_academic_performance: Mixed reading confidence; learn best from short stories, familiar settings, humor, and repetition of key phrases.
student_profile.anticipated_learner_needs_and_barriers: Vocabulary must stay simple with new words defined in a glossary; sentences short; concepts anchored in everyday community life (home, school, market, farm). Learners have never used an AI tool — they meet AI only through story characters.

instructor_preferences.instructor_emphasis_intent: Teach practical problem-solving — asking good questions, checking answers, deciding together — with AI as a thinking partner inside the stories, never as the subject itself. Strengthen reading, critical thinking, and conservation awareness. Never name a real AI product; story characters use ``the assistant'' on an adult's phone, which is sometimes wrong and always checked by people.
instructor_preferences.instructor_style_preferences: Story-based learning: every chapter is a warm, funny, self-contained story in a familiar Kenyan village setting, followed by a glossary, comprehension and critical-thinking questions, and one fully paper-based activity. No lectures, no classroom framing inside the stories.
instructor_preferences.instructor_focus_for_assessment: Comprehension and reflection questions plus paper-based activities (tally charts, question games, role-play, drawing, small family surveys); no exams, no devices.

course_structure.course_learning_outcomes: Ask clear, focused questions about everyday problems; gather and read simple information (tallies, counts, observation); understand that helpers — radios, phone assistants, adults — can be wrong, and check answers against one's own eyes, books, and community knowledge; work with others to plan and improve a small project; speak up and share ideas with confidence; care for the natural world nearby.
course_structure.weekly_schedule_outline:
The Question Notebook: a child starts wondering how the radio knows the weather, meets the teacher's phone assistant, and starts a notebook of good questions
Tomatoes at the Market: which tomatoes sell fastest — a first tally chart at the family market stall
The Assistant's Silly Answer: the phone assistant gives a wrong answer about a local bird, and a child who watches birds catches it — always check
The Goat Mystery: neighbours' goats keep escaping; the friends observe, ask, compare ideas, and solve it with lots of looking and one small assistant hint
The School Garden Plan: the class plans a vegetable garden by asking the right small questions first
Better Together: feedback from older students and parents changes and improves the garden plan
Show and Tell: the class presents the garden to parents, and a nervous child speaks up
What the Notebook Taught: harvest day — questions, checking, asking for help, and deciding together, with a gentle link to the wildlife conservancy nearby

assessment_design.assessment_format_preferences: Per-chapter: 3-4 Think About It questions (comprehension + at least one what-would-YOU-do), one paper-based Try It activity, and a New Words glossary. No exams, no coding, no devices.
assessment_design.assessment_delivery_constraints: Everything is completed on paper in the book or a notebook; nothing requires internet, electricity, or a device.

teaching_constraints.platform_policy_constraints: Print-only delivery: A5 book, layouts must work in full color or grayscale, illustrations effective in black-and-white. Content fully self-contained.
teaching_constraints.ta_support_availability: Read independently or with a teacher/parent; no trained facilitator assumed.
teaching_constraints.instructional_delivery_context: Printed storybook for school and home reading in communities with limited internet connectivity and device availability.

institutional_requirements.program_learning_outcomes: Builds AI literacy, reading confidence, critical thinking, and conservation awareness for upper-primary learners through story-based printed materials.
institutional_requirements.academic_policies_and_institutional_stan: Culturally familiar Kenyan settings and names; a few natural Kiswahili words defined on first use; no real product or brand names; children never approach wildlife or handle anything unsafe in the stories.
institutional_requirements.department_syllabus_requirements: Each chapter must include the story, New Words, Think About It, and Try It sections; the book must open with a contents page.

prior_feedback.historical_course_evaluation_results: No prior offering; this is the first iteration.

storybook.title: Zuri's Big Questions
storybook.subtitle: Stories from Mlima Village
storybook.reading_level: Grade 3-4 reading level: short sentences, common words, warm and funny, repetition of key phrases
storybook.story_bible: SETTING: Mlima Village, a farming community near a wildlife conservancy in southern Kenya. Maize and tomato farms, a weekly market, a school, a river, elephants beyond the conservancy boundary. Mobile money is everyday life; smartphones are scarce and belong to adults. RECURRING CHARACTERS: Zuri, a 10-year-old girl, playful and observant — the protagonist, keeper of a question notebook. Kip, her 9-year-old best friend who loves animals and jokes. Amani, Zuri's thoughtful 14-year-old sister. Mwalimu Grace, the teacher whose phone carries ``the assistant'' and who encourages questions. Baba and Mama, tomato and maize farmers. Mzee Kioko, a village elder with deep local knowledge, friendly skeptic of new technology. Auntie Neema, a wildlife ranger. HOW AI APPEARS: learners have no devices; characters occasionally use an adult's phone assistant, which is helpful but sometimes wrong — characters model asking a clear question, catching a wrong answer, double-checking with elders, books, and their own eyes, and deciding for themselves. VALUES: curiosity, checking before believing, teamwork, respecting elders' knowledge and new tools, girls leading confidently, caring for wildlife. TONE: warm, concrete, funny; illustration placeholders at 1-2 strong visual moments per chapter; scenes must work as black-and-white line art.
